questions.prompt: For a feedback amplifier with DC loop gain \(T_0\), the static (DC) fractional gain error relative to the ideal \(1/f\) is
questions.explanation:
\(G_{cl}=\dfrac1f\cdot\dfrac{T_0}{1+T_0}=\dfrac1f\left(1-\dfrac{1}{1+T_0}\right)\). The shortfall is \(\dfrac{1}{1+T_0}\approx\dfrac{1}{T_0}\).
• \(\dfrac{T_0}{1+T_0}\) is the ratio actual/ideal, not the error.
• \(1/f\) is the ideal gain itself.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a 'dynamic' error in a feedback amplifier, as opposed to a static error?
options: An error caused only by the resistor tolerances
An error that grows with signal frequency (or shows up in transients) because the loop gain \(|T(j\omega)|\) falls at high frequency
An error that exists only at DC
An error caused by the power supply turning on
questions.explanation:
The static error \(1/(1+T_0)\) uses the DC loop gain. At higher frequencies \(|T(j\omega)|\) drops (above the op-amp's dominant pole it falls 20 dB/decade), so the error \(\left|\dfrac{1}{1+T(j\omega)}\right|\) rises, in magnitude and phase. A step response that settles with a time constant is the same effect in the time domain.
• Resistor tolerances set the IDEAL gain \(1/f\), they are not a loop-gain error.

questions.prompt: The loop gain is \(T(jf)=\dfrac{1000}{1+jf/100\ \mathrm{Hz}}\). For a 10 kHz sine, what is the magnitude of the error ratio \(\left|\dfrac{s_{err}}{s_{in}}\right|=\left|\dfrac{1}{1+T}\right|\), in percent?
questions.explanation:
\(T(j10^4)=\dfrac{1000}{1+j100}=\dfrac{1000(1-j100)}{10001}=0.09999-j9.999\).
\(1+T=1.09999-j9.999\), \(|1+T|=10.06\), so \(|1/(1+T)|=9.941\%\).
At DC the error was 0.1%; at 10 kHz, where \(|T|\approx10\), it is about 10%. Common mistake: using \(1/(1+|T|)=9.1\%\), which ignores that \(T\) is almost purely imaginary here.

questions.prompt: The same loop (\(T=\dfrac{1000}{1+jf/100\ \mathrm{Hz}}\)) has \(f=0.01\), so the ideal gain is 100. What is the closed-loop gain MAGNITUDE \(\dfrac1f\left|\dfrac{T}{1+T}\right|\) at 10 kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(\left|\dfrac{T}{1+T}\right|=\dfrac{|0.09999-j9.999|}{|1.09999-j9.999|}=\dfrac{9.9995}{10.059}=0.99407\), so \(|G_{cl}|=99.41\).
Only 0.6% low in magnitude, even though the error ratio is about 10%. The error is mostly in QUADRATURE (90° out of phase), so it mainly shifts the phase instead of shrinking the magnitude.

questions.prompt: A feedback amplifier with ideal gain 10 (\(f=0.1\)) and DC loop gain \(T_0=99\) receives a 1 V input step. What is the output after it has settled?
questions.explanation:
After settling, the DC loop gain applies: \(v_o=\dfrac1f\cdot\dfrac{T_0}{1+T_0}\times1\ \mathrm{V}=10\times\dfrac{99}{100}=9.9\ \mathrm{V}\). A 1% static error remains forever; the transient only decides how fast you get there.
• 10 V would need \(T_0=\infty\).
• 9.09 V is \(10/(1+0.1)\), a mis-use of the formula.
• 10.1 V applies the 1% error with the wrong sign: feedback amplifiers fall SHORT of \(1/f\).

questions.prompt: In the 10 kHz example, the error ratio \(|1/(1+T)|\) was about 10%, but the closed-loop gain magnitude was only 0.6% low. Why the difference?
options: Because the error ratio formula is wrong at high frequencies
Because the ideal gain \(1/f\) changes with frequency
Because 10% and 0.6% are the same error expressed in dB
At 10 kHz \(T\) is almost purely imaginary, so the error adds at nearly \(90^\circ\): it mostly creates a phase error, and the magnitude changes only to second order
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+T}\). With \(T\approx-j10\), the error term is \(\approx\dfrac{1}{1-j10}\approx j0.1\): perpendicular to 1. Adding a perpendicular 0.1 to 1 changes the length by only \(\sqrt{1+0.01}-1\approx0.5\%\) but rotates it by \(\approx5.7^\circ\).
So a single 'percent error' isn't enough at high frequency; magnitude and phase errors behave differently.

questions.prompt: For the same loop at 10 kHz (\(T=\dfrac{1000}{1+j100}\)), what is the phase of the closed-loop gain relative to the ideal, \(\angle\dfrac{T}{1+T}\), in degrees?
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=\dfrac{0.09999-j9.999}{1.09999-j9.999}\). Angles: numerator \(-89.43^\circ\), denominator \(-83.72^\circ\); difference \(=-5.705^\circ\).
About \(-5.7^\circ\) of phase lag (\(\approx-\tan^{-1}(1/|T|)\)), while the magnitude was only 0.6% low.

questions.prompt: An op-amp is modeled as a pure integrator \(A=\omega_u/(j\omega)\) (infinite DC gain), with \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and \(f=0.1\). Which describes its errors?
options: Zero error at every frequency, since the gain is infinite
A static error of 10%, constant with frequency
Zero static error, but a dynamic error of about \(|1/(1+T)|\approx10\%\) at 10 kHz, where \(|T|\approx10\)
Infinite error at DC
questions.explanation:
\(T=Af=\dfrac{f\,\omega_u}{j\omega}\): infinite at DC, so the static error \(1/(1+T_0)\) is 0. At 10 kHz, \(|T|=0.1\times10^6/10^4=10\) and \(|1/(1+T)|=1/|1-j10|\approx9.95\%\).
'Infinite gain' only at DC: the trap is equating infinite DC gain with perfect accuracy at all frequencies.

questions.prompt: Preview of the source follower. Later you will see a transistor follower whose voltage gain has the form \(\dfrac{T}{1+T}\), i.e. a feedback loop with \(f=1\) and loop gain \(T\). If \(T=9\), what is its gain?
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=\dfrac{9}{10}=0.9\). With \(f=1\) the ideal gain is 1, and the static error \(1/(1+T)=10\%\) explains why such followers have gain a bit below 1. More loop gain gives a better follower.

questions.prompt: Preview of source degeneration (local feedback). A stage has forward gain \(G=50\) and feedback that makes \(T=4\), so its gain is \(G/(1+T)=10\). The device's \(G\) increases by 2% (to 51, with \(f\) unchanged). By what percent does the closed-loop gain change?
questions.explanation:
\(f=T/G=0.08\). New gain \(=\dfrac{51}{1+51\times0.08}=\dfrac{51}{5.08}=10.039\), a change of \(0.394\%\).
Sensitivity is reduced by \(1+T=5\): \(2\%/5=0.4\%\). Degeneration in transistor amplifiers uses exactly this trade (gain for stability against device variation).

questions.prompt: Preview of transistor amplifiers. A transistor gain stage has a voltage gain that varies by \(\pm30\%\) with temperature and manufacturing. You need a gain accurate to \(\pm0.3\%\). Using only ideas from feedback errors, what works?
options: Use the stage open-loop and select parts carefully
Make a stage with about \(100\times\) more gain than needed and close a loop with a precise \(f\), so \(T\approx100\) divides the variation by \(\sim100\)
Close a loop with \(T\approx1\)
Add a second identical stage in series to average the errors
questions.explanation: Closed-loop sensitivity is the open-loop sensitivity divided by \(1+T\): \(30\%/101\approx0.3\%\). That requires excess forward gain (\(G=T/f\)) which is then 'spent' on accuracy. A cascade without feedback multiplies variations instead of averaging them; \(T\approx1\) only halves them.
